Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Secondary bacterial infections complicating allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) are uncommon but can be serious given the expansile nature of the disease which can thin and erode the bone separating the sinuses from the brain and orbits. Zoonotic pathogens are rarely implicated as pathogens. CASE REPORT: A 21-year-old African American male with several years of progressive nasal obstruction, facial pressure, and hyposmia, presented emergently with acute left eye pain and swelling, diplopia, afferent pupillary defect and inferior visual field deficit. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated acute on chronic sinusitis with a left orbital abscess. The patient underwent emergent endoscopic sinus surgery with left orbitotomy and drainage of the orbital abscess. Intraoperative findings, pathology, cultures, and allergy testing were reviewed demonstrating AFRS and a novel zoonotic bacterium, Streptococcus halichoeri. CONCLUSIONS: This case represents the first otolaryngologic case of S. halichoeri infection, a severe and complicated sinus and orbital infection. It is unclear if the severity of this infection was a consequence of the unusual pathogen, of the long-term thinning of the bone around the orbit, or both. Although AFRS is not considered an infection, secondary bacterial infection may occur and cause severe complications. Early surgical intervention and culture-directed therapy are essential in managing complicated sinonasal diseases.

item.title: Wildfire Air Pollution Exposure and Head and Neck Cancer Incidence.
item.dc:creator: Jung YS, Yu SE, Nadeau KC, Cramer J, Xu MJ, Mitchell MB, Chiang S, Ruan M, Lee SE
item.description:
Authors: Jung YS, Yu SE, Nadeau KC, Cramer J, Xu MJ, Mitchell MB, Chiang S, Ruan M, Lee SE
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.70874
Published: 2026-Oct-13

Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine the association between wildfire-specific particulate matter 2.5 (wPM2.5) exposure and the overall and site-specific incidences of head and neck and aerodigestive cancer (HNC). STUDY DESIGN: Epidemiological retrospective cohort analysis. METHODS: HNC incidence data were derived from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program (2016-2022). The relationship between county-level wPM2.5 exposure metrics and HNC incidence rates were examined using a distributed lag non-linear model, adjusting for health behaviors (tobacco/alcohol use, diet, exercise, and sexual activity), demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity), population size, and year, with county as a random effect. Lag effects were analyzed over 10 years. HNC subsites included nasal/sinus/ear, nasopharynx, oral cavity, oropharynx (stratified by p16 status), hypopharynx, and larynx. RESULTS: Higher wildfire-specific PM2.5 exposure was associated with increased cumulative HNC incidence over 0-10-year lags, with a cumulative relative risk (cRR) of 1.06 (95% CI: 1.04-1.09) per additional smoke exceedance day, 1.41 (1.24-1.60) for any annual exposure, and 1.23 (1.13-1.33) per percentage-point increase in days above 5 μg/m3. When stratified by p16 status, significant associations were noted for p16-positive, p16-negative, and p16-unknown tumors. CONCLUSIONS: Higher frequency, intensity, or persistence of wildfire-smoke exposure is associated with increased HNC risk, with the strongest associations driven by long-term exposures.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the prognostic relevance of human papillomavirus (HPV) in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). METHODS: The National Cancer Data Base (NCDB) was used to query patients with NPC and available HPV testing data between 2010 and 2017. Logistic regression was performed to predict factors associated with HPV testing and HPV positivity. Overall survival (OS) was evaluated using Kaplan Meier analysis between HPV-positive versus HPV-negative cohorts. Univariate and multivariate analyses using Cox proportional hazards modeling were performed to assess for factors associated with OS. Kaplan Meier analysis revealed improved OS among HPV-positive patients with keratinizing subtype of NPC (log rank p < 0.001). Abstract:
PURPOSE: Quality assurance (QA) of auto-segmentations is necessary for safe clinical deployment. Deep learning models are optimised for data similar to their training set, but reliability drops with out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. This study evaluates whether uncertainty quantification (UQ) can detect OOD inputs arising from distribution shift in head and neck organ of interest (OOI) auto-segmentation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Monte Carlo dropout-based uncertainty scores and geometric accuracy of nnU-Net models were evaluated in two experiments. First, as a proof-of-concept, we assessed whether uncertainty scores detect metal artefact (N = 10) from non-artefact cases (N = 10) on a baseline model (mixed training data, N = 620) and a no-metal model (artefact-free training data, N = 620). Second, in a clinically realistic experiment, we split a fine-tuning dataset by uncertainty score to obtain a narrow model (low-uncertainty cases, N = 21) and a broad model (high-uncertainty cases, N = 21). A held-out test set (N = 76) evaluated whether segmentation accuracy differed between uncertainty categories. RESULTS: Both experiments showed that uncertainty scores reflect the learned training distribution. In the supervised experiment, the no-metal model demonstrated greater uncertainty score separation between artefact and non-artefact cases (1.1 × 105 vs 0.6 × 105) than the baseline model (1.1 × 105 vs 0.8 × 105). In the unsupervised experiment, the narrow model performed significantly better on certain than uncertain cases (p = 0.04), while no difference was seen for the broad model (p = 0.34), which did include these cases in training. CONCLUSIONS: Uncertainty quantification can detect distribution shifts in radiotherapy auto-segmentation. This could support automated QA workflows by identifying in-distribution cases and enabling the application of specialised models.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: We conducted a randomized phase II trial to evaluate whether adding erlotinib to platinum/docetaxel improves clinical outcomes in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas, building on our previous single-arm phase II trial. Abstract:
PURPOSE: Optimizing treatment in HPV-associated OPSCC remains challenging, as current TNM- and smoking-based risk stratification inadequately captures tumor biological heterogeneity, highlighting the need for more prognostic biomarkers. IS quantified CD3⁺ and CD8⁺ densities in tumor cores and invasive margins, with cut-offs defined in the training cohort and validated across cohorts. Associations with disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), and time to recurrence (TTR) were assessed, alongside 3'RNA-seq and sequential immunofluorescence profiling. RESULTS: Median age 65; 80% male; 74% smokers; 66% T1-2; 82% N0-1. IS-High patients had superior 3-year DFS across cohorts (all log-rank P < .05). Multivariable analysis identified IS-Low as the independent prognostic factor with the largest adjusted effect size for DFS (HR 9.03; 95% CI: 4.02-20.31; P < .001). The combined IS-clinical model showed better DFS prediction than the clinical-only model (C-index 0.82 vs 0.70; P < .0001). Similar results were observed for TTR and OS. By identifying biologically distinct risk groups, IS may enable biomarker-guided, risk-adapted treatment strategies, including treatment de-escalation and intensification.

item.title: Differential impact of tumor-derived ESR1 mutations on elacestrant benefit in metastatic breast cancer.
item.dc:creator: Sledge GW, Xiu J, Fuqua S, Ribeiro JR, McArthur H, Oberley MJ, Radovich M, Spetzler D, Kaklamani V
item.description:
Authors: Sledge GW, Xiu J, Fuqua S, Ribeiro JR, McArthur H, Oberley MJ, Radovich M, Spetzler D, Kaklamani V
Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research | DOI: 10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-26-2215
Published: 2026-Oct-13

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: ESR1 mutations are a well-established mechanism of endocrine therapy resistance in estrogen receptor (ER)-positive metastatic breast cancer and are a biomarker for treatment benefit from oral selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs) such as elacestrant. However, variant-specific and context-dependent effects on therapy response remain poorly understood. METHODS: Breast tumors carrying ESR1 mutations that underwent DNA sequencing at Caris Life Sciences were studied (n=3,344), with whole-transcriptome sequencing available for a subset (n=1,663). Time-on-treatment (TOT) was obtained from insurance claims and defined as the interval from initiation to discontinuation of elacestrant. Cox proportional hazards models were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs), and log-rank tests assessed statistical significance. RESULTS: ESR1 mutation frequency increased with longer duration of prior endocrine therapy including combined treatment regimens, particularly those including CDK4/6 inhibitors. Heterogeneity in treatment benefit was observed across ESR1 variants. Tumors harboring ESR1-L536 mutations demonstrated reduced elacestrant benefit, with significantly shorter TOT compared to more common mutations such as Y537 and D538G (HR=2.089, p=0.001). L536-mutated tumors had lower expression of GREB1, a key estrogen-responsive gene, and reduced enrichment of estrogen response pathways, suggesting reduced ER pathway activation compared to other variants. Additionally, patients with multiple ESR1 mutations had significantly shorter TOT compared to those with single mutations (adjusted HR=1.62, p=0.038). CONCLUSIONS: ESR1 mutations are likely not functionally equivalent in their impact on elacestrant benefit. These findings highlight the importance of variant-specific stratification in optimizing endocrine therapy and suggest that biomarkers of ER signaling activity may further refine patient selection for SERD treatment.

item.title: Investigation of salivary microRNAs as non-invasive biomarkers for weaning stress in piglets: A preliminary study.
item.dc:creator: Jeong GH, Park SJ, Lim KS
item.description:
Authors: Jeong GH, Park SJ, Lim KS
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360727
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42868144



Abstract:
Weaning exposes piglets to abrupt nutritional and environmental changes that induce physiological stress. Saliva, unlike serum or tissue samples, enables repeated and stress-free sampling, making it a practical biological matrix for monitoring early-life adaptation. To evaluate whether salivary microRNAs (miRNAs) can serve as non-invasive indicators of these responses, we profiled miRNA expression in saliva collected from suckling and weaning piglets. Small RNA sequencing was conducted to detect salivary miRNAs and a total of 41 differentially expressed miRNAs (DEMs) were detected between the two groups, with 20 showing highly expression and 21 showing lowly expression in weaning piglets. Several of these DEMs have been previously associated with immune activity, inflammatory regulation, oxidative stress responses, and disease processes, highlighting their biological relevance during the weaning transition. Functional annotation of predicted target genes revealed enrichment in pathways such as TGF-beta, HIF-1, and AMPK signaling, as well as autophagy-related processes. These pathways are known to play key roles in stress adaptation, cellular metabolism, and immune modulation. These findings suggest that salivary miRNA profiles may reflect molecular changes associated with the weaning transition and may serve as candidate non-invasive indicators of physiological stress and health status in piglets. This approach may provide a basis for future development of saliva-based monitoring strategies after validation in larger cohorts and cost-effective targeted assays.

item.title: Personalized assessment of high-definition slow-oscillatory transcranial direct current stimulation (so-tDCS) in older adults with sleep and subjective cognitive complaints: A study protocol for a randomized clinical trial.
item.dc:creator: Lu H, Ni X, Yang NS, Yuen YS, Gong Y, Ma SL
item.description:
Authors: Lu H, Ni X, Yang NS, Yuen YS, Gong Y, Ma SL
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360573
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42868122



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) is increasingly recognized as an early and potentially modifiable stage in the trajectory of neurodegenerative diseases. In older adults with SCD, untreated sleep disturbances may accelerate the neurodegenerative process, potentially via mechanisms involving amyloid-beta accumulation, and contribute to more rapid cognitive deterioration. Currently, non-pharmacological treatment options that concurrently manage SCD and sleep disturbances remain scarce. High-definition slow-oscillatory transcranial direct current stimulation (so-tDCS) is an emerging, frequency-specific neuromodulation technique designed to enhance brain health and cognition. METHODS AND DESIGN: This is a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled clinical trial. Right-handed Chinese older adults with SCD and sleep disturbances will be randomly assigned to receive either high-definition 0.75 Hz so-tDCS or sham stimulation over a 4-week intervention period, with 40 participants per group. Outcome measures, including galvanic skin response, subjective cognitive complaints, sleep quality, salivary amyloid-beta levels, and domain-specific cognitive performance, will be evaluated at four time points: baseline, week 4 (immediately post‑intervention), and follow‑up at weeks 8 and 12. CONCLUSIONS: Personalized neurophysiological signals, namely electrode-skin impedance, will be monitored using state-of-the-art measurement during so-tDCS. The successful implement of this signal will provide researchers with access to an "add-on" setting that enables them to easily, quickly and quantitatively evaluate real-time neurophysiological signals, thereby facilitating the incorporation of transcranial brain stimulation into clinical practice. item.title: Maternal opioid prescriptions and subsequent risk of hospital admission in offspring in South Korea: A nationwide birth cohort study.
item.dc:creator: Kim HJ, Yim Y, Nehs CJ, Park J, Kim ES, Cho SJ, Fond G, Boyer L, Kang J, Yon DK
item.description:
Authors: Kim HJ, Yim Y, Nehs CJ, Park J, Kim ES, Cho SJ, Fond G, Boyer L, Kang J, Yon DK
Journal: PLoS medicine | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1004829
Published: 2026-Oct-01
PMID: 42868097



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prenatal opioid exposure may disrupt infant development and immune system function, potentially increasing long-term susceptibility to hospital admissions. Thus, we aimed to investigate the association between prenatal opioid exposure and the risk of hospital admission in children. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We established a population-based birth cohort in South Korea by linking mothers and children using National Health Insurance Service data and followed from January 1, 2009, to December 31, 2023. We constructed propensity score (PS)-matched and sibling comparison cohorts and performed a multi-pronged approach, including dose-dependent and time-attenuation analyses. All 5,249,429 individuals with eligible children born between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2017, were included (2,236,167 mothers and 3,013,262 children). Infants were followed up for up to 14 years, depending on birth year. Prenatal exposure to opioids was defined as maternal receipt of two or more prescriptions within any given trimester. Adjusted incidence rate ratio (aIRR) of hospital admission among children with prenatal opioid exposure was estimated for causes including infections, non-infectious respiratory conditions, non-infectious gastrointestinal conditions, oral cavity diseases, injuries/external causes, and non-infectious genitourinary conditions. Analyses were adjusted for maternal age at delivery, infant sex, region of residence, household income level, birth season, parity, severe maternal morbidity score, number of outpatient visits and hospital admissions in the year before pregnancy, preterm birth, low birth weight, delivery type, year of delivery, maternal history of substance use and neuropsychiatric disorders, and plurality. Of the 2,928,186 children, we identified 2,809,515 (51.4% male) and 118,671 (51.3% male) infants without and with prenatal opioid exposure, respectively. The rate of hospital admissions in children with prenatal opioid exposure was 28% higher in the PS-matched cohort (aIRR 1.28 [95% CI 1.28, 1.29]; p < 0.001). The association was attenuated in the sibling comparison cohort, indicating the potential influence of shared familial factors, but remained statistically significant (aIRR 1.08 [95% CI 1.07, 1.10]; p < 0.001). Hospital admission rates in children increased in a dose-dependent manner with maternal opioid dose and duration of opioid prescriptions (low-dose exposure: aIRR 1.19 [95% CI 1.19, 1.20]; p < 0.001; high-dose exposure: aIRR 1.40 [95% CI 1.39, 1.41]; p < 0.001). Prenatal opioid exposure was significantly associated with increased rates of hospital admission across several causes of morbidities, including infections, respiratory non-infections, oral cavity, gastrointestinal non-infections, genitourinary non-infections, and injury/external conditions. These associations between prenatal opioid exposure and hospital admission rates in children diminished with age but remained evident up to five years of age. The main limitations of this study's methodology include the use of prescription records, which may not fully capture actual medication intake, and residual confounding that cannot be entirely excluded. CONCLUSIONS: In this nationwide birth cohort study, maternal opioid prescription during pregnancy was associated with a substantial increase in the risk of hospital admissions in the offspring across various causes of morbidities. Although the attenuated estimates in the sibling comparison analysis suggest that familial factors may partly explain this association, these findings may inform postnatal monitoring and management strategies for children born to mothers who received opioid prescriptions during pregnancy.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: Reducing the time to treatment improves outcomes, including survival, in patients with head and neck cancer (HNC). METHODS: All patients with newly diagnosed HNC in 2008 were compared with those diagnosed in 2016 before and after the agreement with referring hospitals to immediately refer patients based on clinical suspicion of cancer and refrain from any additional diagnostic procedures. item.title: Pathological characteristics rather than thyroid size predict incidental parathyroidectomy during thyroid surgery.
item.dc:creator: Aydın HT, Gökdere OG, Aydın A
item.description:
Authors: Aydın HT, Gökdere OG, Aydın A
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10645-7

PMID: 42867665



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Incidental parathyroidectomy (IP) is a recognized event during thyroid surgery and may contribute to postoperative hypocalcemia and impaired parathyroid function. Although several clinical and operative factors associated with IP have been described, the contribution of thyroid size-related characteristics remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the association between thyroid size-related parameters, clinicopathological characteristics, and the occurrence of IP. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent thyroidectomy between January 2021 and December 2025 at a tertiary referral center. Patients with primary parathyroid disease were excluded. Demographic, operative, pathological, and thyroid size-related variables, including dominant nodule diameter, thyroid specimen weight, and thyroid lobe dimensions, were analyzed. Associations with incidental parathyroidectomy were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses. The multivariable model included age, sex, malignant thyroid pathology, Hashimoto thyroiditis, multinodular goiter/nodular hyperplasia, extent of thyroidectomy, and central neck dissection. RESULTS: The study included 1,049 patients, of whom 125 (11.9%) had incidental parathyroidectomy. Dominant nodule diameter and thyroid specimen weight were not significantly associated with IP in available-case analyses. Increasing largest thyroid lobe diameter was associated with lower odds of IP in univariable analysis, although this association was not robust after adjustment. In the multivariable analysis, malignant thyroid pathology (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.47; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.49-4.09; p < 0.001), multinodular goiter/nodular hyperplasia (aOR, 2.31; 95% CI, 1.11-4.80; p = 0.025), and female sex (aOR, 1.88; 95% CI, 1.01-3.50; p = 0.045) were independently associated with higher odds of IP. Hashimoto thyroiditis (aOR, 1.53; 95% CI, 0.96-2.44; p = 0.072), central neck dissection (aOR, 1.55; 95% CI, 0.98-2.45; p = 0.058), and total/bilateral thyroidectomy (aOR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.34-1.06; p = 0.079) were not independently associated with IP. CONCLUSIONS: Malignant thyroid pathology and multinodular goiter/nodular hyperplasia were independently associated with higher odds of incidental parathyroidectomy after adjustment for demographic and operative factors, including central neck dissection. Female sex was also associated with higher odds of IP, whereas Hashimoto thyroiditis did not retain statistical significance after multivariable adjustment. Thyroid size-related parameters showed no consistent independent association with IP. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the retrospective design, incomplete data for some thyroid size-related parameters, and the possibility of residual confounding.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: To define the most distal entry point (MDEP) of the pectoral branch in adult Chinese males, integrate it into a standardised Landmark-Axis-Plane (LAP) skeletonisation workflow for the pectoralis major island flap, and describe its clinical performance under IDEAL Stage 2a. item.title: The clinical outcomes and overall survival in patients with mucoepidermoid and adenoid cystic carcinoma of the salivary glands: A comparative analysis of long-term outcomes.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC) and adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC) are the two most common salivary gland malignancies, but differ substantially in biological behavior, recurrence patterns and long-term prognosis. item.title: Artificial intelligence-based prediction of cerebrospinal fluid leak in skull base surgery: a scoping review.
item.dc:creator: Aydogmus E, Atalay Erdogan B
item.description:
Authors: Aydogmus E, Atalay Erdogan B
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10667-1
Published: 2026-Oct-13
PMID: 42867660



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak remains one of the most significant complications of skull base surgery, particularly in endoscopic endonasal and transsphenoidal approaches. Accurate risk stratification may improve surgical planning and reconstruction strategies. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based models have been increasingly investigated for CSF leak prediction; however, the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous. This scoping review aimed to map the current literature and summarize data sources, modeling approaches, validation strategies, and reported performance. METHODS: This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidance. Eligibility was structured using the Population-Concept-Context framework. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for English-language studies published from 2019 to 2025. Two authors independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts and independently charted data using a standardized table; disagreements were resolved by consensus. Eligible original human studies applied AI/ML to predict perioperative surgical CSF leak or to derive an imaging biomarker for identifying spontaneous lateral skull-base CSF leak/encephalocele relevant to surgical assessment. No formal protocol was prepared or registered. RESULTS: Fifty-five records were identified, and nine primary studies met the eligibility criteria after duplicate removal and full-text assessment. Six studies predicted intraoperative CSF leak, two predicted postoperative leak, and one evaluated a deep-learning-derived CT biomarker for identifying spontaneous lateral skull-base CSF leak or encephalocele relevant to surgical assessment. Three studies used classical machine-learning methods, four used predominantly deep neural-network or convolutional-neural-network approaches, one compared classical models with a feedforward neural network, and one used a BERT-based natural-language-processing model. One study reported prospective temporal validation; none reported independent external validation at another institution. Among studies reporting AUC, values ranged from 0.69 to 1.00; accuracy, where reported, ranged from 70% to 98.33%. CONCLUSIONS: AI-based prediction of CSF leak is a promising but evolving field. Methodological heterogeneity and the absence of independent external validation constrain clinical translation. Future studies should prioritize standardized outcomes, multicenter datasets, and prospective validation to support integration into clinical decision-making.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate hearing outcomes following early simultaneous oral and intratympanic corticosteroid therapy in patients with sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL). RESULTS: Median baseline PTA improved from 85 dB to 56 dB one month after treatment, corresponding to a median improvement of 28 dB (p < 0.0001). Median SDS increased from 0% to 80% (p < 0.0001). No statistically significant differences in hearing improvement were observed according to treatment initiation time, age group, or baseline hearing classification. CONCLUSION: Early simultaneous combined oral and intratympanic corticosteroid therapy was associated with significant improvements in PTA and SDS in this cohort of patients with SSHL without major adverse events observed during follow-up. Abstract:
PURPOSE: Thyroid cancers often present as nodules, with fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) and ultrasonography as the primary diagnostic tools. Given the variability in clinical approaches and the lack of consensus guidelines, ultrasonography has become increasingly important, particularly for indeterminate cytology. We aim to assess the clinical utility and diagnostic performance of the ACR TI-RADS (American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System), together with cytopathological subtypes, in predicting malignancy in atypia of undetermined significance (AUS) cases. METHODS: In this prospective, single-centre study conducted over 30 months, all AUS cases underwent preoperative ultrasonographic evaluation using the ACR TI-RADS, and had postoperative histopathological results. RESULTS: Seventy-one nodules from 67 patients were included. The median age was 51 years (range: 12-71). The overall malignancy rate was 20%. Among the nodules, 26 (37%) were classified as the nuclear atypia, and 45 (63%) as other atypia. The ACR TI-RADS score had a strong association with malignancy (p = 0.025). The presence and type of echogenic foci were associated with malignancy (p = 0.001). The malignancy rates for TR3, TR4, and TR5 nodules were 21%, 8%, and 55% respectively. CONCLUSION: The ACR TI-RADS was significantly associated with malignancy in both the overall AUS cohort and the nuclear atypia subgroup. The relatively high number of follicular thyroid carcinoma cases may have masked the predictive value of ultrasonography. The presence of peripheral calcifications was significantly associated with malignancy. Although the sample size was adequate by power analysis, larger cohorts would further strengthen these findings.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine whether intraoperative autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) reduces postoperative pain and haemorrhage and enhances wound healing after tonsillectomy, while critically evaluating the limitations that affect clinical translation and future applications. METHODS: Five databases were searched through 3 July 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing PRP with no PRP, placebo, or an untreated contralateral fossa. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty using GRADE. Random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment were used for pain and healing outcomes; sparse haemorrhage outcomes were analysed using Mantel-Haenszel common-effect models with sensitivity analyses. Parallel-group and split-mouth trials were analysed separately. RESULTS: Twelve randomized trials including 723 patients were included, with 11 contributing quantitative data. PRP was associated with reduced pain on postoperative day (POD) 1 (MD -1.21, 95% CI -2.01 to -0.40) and POD 3 (MD -1.12, 95% CI -2.10 to -0.14), although effects were heterogeneous and transient. Primary haemorrhage showed a favourable common-effect estimate (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.07-0.80), but this was based on only 12 events and was not confirmed by random-effects sensitivity analysis. Complete healing did not significantly differ between groups (RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.59-3.06). CONCLUSION: PRP may provide a modest early analgesic effect after tonsillectomy, but current evidence does not demonstrate a consistent improvement in haemostasis or mucosal healing. Future research should focus on standardized PRP characterization, patient-level comparative trials, and direct evaluation of whether PRP improves tissue regeneration compared with other biomaterial-based approaches.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: Acquired nasopharyngeal stenosis (NPS) is a rare but serious complication following tonsillectomy or laser-assisted uvulopalatoplasty, leading to choking sensation and impaired nasal breathing. This study aimed to describe a modified pharyngoplasty technique and report its short-term outcomes. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on five patients with acquired NPS who underwent the procedure between 2017 and 2025. All cases were refractory to conservative treatment. The surgical technique involved symmetrical mucosal flaps combined with absorbable barbed sutures to achieve stable expansion of the pharyngeal airway. RESULTS: All patients showed rapid improvement in choking sensation and nasal breathing postoperatively. Normal speech and oral intake were possible from the day after surgery. During follow-up (5 months-2 years), no restenosis or major complications were observed, and endoscopic findings confirmed sustained airway patency. CONCLUSION: This technique can be performed safely in a single session without muscle resection or stenting and demonstrated favorable short-term outcomes. It may represent a practical surgical option for selected patients with acquired NPS. Further studies are required to confirm long-term efficacy.

item.title: Appropriate extent of endoscopic sinus surgery brings favorable therapeutic outcomes to chronic rhinosinusitis patients.
item.dc:creator: Tran T, Samuthpongtorn J, Seresirikachorn K, Chitsuthipakorn W, Hoang MP, Tran LV, Le MTQ, Anggraini D, Wardani RS, Mohamad S, et al.

Published: 2026-Oct-13

Abstract:
PURPOSE: The optimal extent of endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) for patients with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) remains undetermined. This study aimed to evaluate postoperative outcomes when the extent of ESS is concordant with the underlying pathophysiology. METHODS: This study enrolled 116 patients with CRS scheduled for three categories of ESS: limited ESS, full-house ESS, and extended ESS. Concordant ESS was defined as (1) limited ESS performed for patients requiring ventilation and drainage and (2) either full-house ESS or extended ESS performed for patients requiring access for topical therapies. Postoperative outcomes included symptom visual analogue scale (VAS), the Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22), and endoscopic scores. RESULTS: At one year, patients receiving concordant ESS achieved superior outcomes in symptom VAS (mean difference [MD] 1.38; 95% CI 0.62-2.15; P < 0.01), SNOT-22 (MD 22.73; 95% CI 15.46-30.00; P < 0.01), and endoscopic scores (MD 6.48; 95% CI 1.96-11.00; P < 0.01). When ESS was performed to improve ventilation and drainage, limited ESS and full-house ESS brought comparable outcomes. Limited ESS achieved better outcomes than extended ESS in SNOT-22 (MD - 21.05; 95% CI - 38.72 to - 3.37; P = 0.02). When ESS aimed to provide access for topical therapies, SNOT-22 was greater improved by full-house (MD 21.32; 95% CI 10.01-32.62; P < 0.01) and extended ESS (MD 26.16; 95% CI 14.85-37.46; P < 0.01) compared to limited ESS. CONCLUSIONS: The extent of ESS should be tailored to the underlying pathophysiology. Limited and full-house ESS are appropriate to improve ventilation. Full-house and extended ESS provide better outcomes when access for topical therapies is required.

item.title: Gasless endoscopic thyroidectomy via the transsubclavian approach: comparable safety and superior anterior cervical function preservation.
item.dc:creator: Huang C, Wang W, Yao J
item.description:
Authors: Huang C, Wang W, Yao J
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10641-x
Published: 2026-Oct-13

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Conventional open thyroidectomy (COT) for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) frequently induces anterior cervical dysfunction and conspicuous scarring. The gasless endoscopic thyroidectomy via the transsubclavian approach (GETTSA) offers technical simplicity and superior cosmesis. This study assessed whether GETTSA provides adequate completeness of resection and effectiveness compared with COT while achieving superior preservation of anterior cervical function. METHODS: This prospective cohort study enrolled consecutive patients with unilateral PTC who underwent hemithyroidectomy between 2023 and 2025, with 37 in the GETTSA group and 65 in the COT group. Baseline and perioperative data were prospectively collected. Scar appearance and anterior cervical function were assessed using the Vancouver Scar Scale (VSS), Neck Impairment Score (NIS), Swallowing Impairment Score (SIS), and Voice Impairment Score (VIS) at 1, 3, and 6 months. Group comparisons were performed using t‑tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, or chi‑square tests, and generalized estimating equations (GEE) evaluated longitudinal group, time, and interaction effects. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics between the two groups were comparable. GETTSA had a longer operative time (P < 0.001) but less intraoperative blood loss (P = 0.002); hospital stay was slightly longer (P < 0.001). Parathyroid autotransplantation rates were higher in GETTSA (P < 0.001), yet postoperative PTH and calcium levels were similar. GEE demonstrated significant group and time effects for VSS, NIS, and SIS (all P < 0.001), with significant group‑by‑time interactions (P = 0.048, P = 0.026, and P < 0.001, respectively), indicating better and faster recovery in the GETTSA group. VIS showed a significant time effect (P < 0.001), but no group effect (P = 0.333) or interaction (P = 0.637). R0 resection was achieved in all patients, and no major procedure‑related complications occurred. CONCLUSION: GETTSA offers superior functional and cosmetic outcomes-notably improved swallowing function, better scar appearance, and reduced neck discomfort-with less intraoperative bleeding, comparable parathyroid safety, and adequate completeness of resection. Long‑term oncological surveillance is ongoing.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To explore the relationship between recurrent otitis media (ROM), chronic media otitis with effusion (COM), and laryngopharyngeal reflux disease (LPRD) in pediatric populations. DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases. REVIEW METHODS: Two investigators independently screened papers with PRISMA guidelines considering the following primary outcomes: LPRD prevalence in pediatric ROM and COM, diagnostic methods used, and detection rates of gastroduodenal markers in middle ear effusions. Two random-effects meta-analyses were performed to estimate the pooled prevalence of pepsin/pepsinogen detection in middle ear effusions and to compare pepsin concentrations between COM/ROM patients and controls using standardized mean differences (Hedges' g). RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included (2070 pediatric patients). The cumulated gastroesophageal reflux disease prevalence in COM children was estimated to 50.7%, while 27.6% of children reported pharyngeal reflux events. Fifteen studies measured pepsin in effusions, reporting a pooled detection prevalence of 72.5% (95% CI: 53.7%-88.0%), rising to 85.6% with ELISA-based methods versus 17.9% with enzymatic assays. The pooled standardized mean difference in pepsin concentration between OME patients and controls was large and significant (Hedges' g = 1.92, 95% CI: 0.58-3.25, P = .005). Alkaline-activated gastroduodenal mediators were assessed in 3 studies, with detection rates ranging from 39.6% to 100% for trypsin and from 32% to 42% for bile salts. CONCLUSION: Gastroduodenal biomarkers are present in middle ear effusions of children with COM and ROM. Future prospective transversal studies exploring alkaline-activated enzymes and bile salts in effusion of children with documented pharyngeal reflux events are needed.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (OHNS) residency remains highly competitive, with persistent disparities in applicant representation. This study presents a cross-sectional analysis of OHNS residency and faculty demographics using 2025 program rosters, evaluating degree type (MD vs DO), geographic distribution, and leadership influence. STUDY DESIGN: A cross-sectional review. SETTING: All US ACGME-accredited OHNS residency programs, with data collected in 2024 to 2025. METHODS: Demographic data were collected on OHNS faculty and residents, including post-graduate year (PGY) 1 through PGY5 trainees at the time of data collection, corresponding to entry years from 2020 to 2024 across all US ACGME-accredited residency programs. Data was extracted from official program websites, FREIDA, ACGME, NRMP, and social media. Programs with incomplete data, those using the military match, and non-accredited sites were excluded. Descriptive statistics, χ2 tests, and correlation analyses were performed (p < .05). RESULTS: Of 131 programs, 125 were analyzed at the program level and 121 at the faculty level. DO residents were concentrated in Michigan (59%), Ohio (50%), and Oklahoma (50%). DO representation correlated with DO faculty (r = .82, p < .0001), DO program director (r = .95, p < .0001), and former AOA program designation (r = .92, p < .0001). DO residents remain underrepresented and geographically concentrated, with representation strongly associated with osteopathic faculty presence, program leadership, and prior AOA affiliation.

item.title: Potential Benefit of Effective Implementation of Timely Postoperative Radiation for Head and Neck Cancer.
item.dc:creator: Luong PQ, Hartman AL, Velez-Velez LM, Mazul A, Massa ST

Authors: Luong PQ, Hartman AL, Velez-Velez LM, Mazul A, Massa ST

Published: 2026-Oct-13

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the potential benefit of survival of receiving timely postoperative radiation therapy (PORT) for head and neck cancer. STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort. SETTING: National Cancer Database from 2004 to 2020. METHODS: Patients with a diagnosis of human papilloma virus (HPV)-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma who received adjuvant radiation were included. Exposure groups included timely PORT or delayed PORT (≤42 or >42 days from surgery to radiotherapy, respectively). The primary outcome was 5-year overall survival (OS). Inverse probability weighted models were used to estimate OS in the counter-factual scenario that all patients started radiation within 6 weeks while adjusting for confounding. Observed OS was for the entire cohort, while predicted OS was for the generated model of universal timely PORT within 6 weeks. Survival analyses were replicated for demographic and clinical subgroups. RESULTS: In total, 58,184 patients were included. Patients were mostly male, white, and non-Hispanic. The observed average 5-year OS was similar to the predicted OS (observed 0.58, 95% CI: 0.57-0.578; predicted 0.58, 95% CI: 0.57-0.59). The largest predicted benefit for timely PORT was seen in privately insured, white, rural, males, and with hypopharyngeal and stage IV cancer, though confidence intervals included the null hypothesis. Conversely, black patients were predicted to have a decline in OS with timely PORT (observed 0.54, 95% CI 0.53-0.56; predicted 0.50, 95% CI 0.46-0.52). CONCLUSION: For the overall cohort and other subgroups, even if optimally implemented, timely PORT is not predicted to improve OS. Modeling outcomes can guide resource allocation to the most impactful interventions.

item.title: Mitochondrially Encoded Cytochrome C Oxidase 1, a Hypoxia- and Lactylation-Related Gene, Acts as a Tumor Suppressor and Therapeutic Target in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

item.description:
Authors: Zuo YD, Dong SD, Li JH, Li JC
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70475

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aberrant expression of mitochondrially encoded Cytochrome c Oxidase Subunit 1 (MT-CO1) has increasingly been associated with tumor invasiveness and adverse clinical outcomes across multiple malignancies. However, its functional role and regulatory mechanisms in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remain poorly understood. METHODS: Transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were integrated to identify genes consistently dysregulated across datasets. Candidate prognostic genes were subsequently prioritized using Cox proportional hazards regression in combination with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. A multi-omics validation framework was then applied, encompassing analysis of MT-CO1 expression in OSCC, protein-level validation using the Human Protein Atlas, and evaluation of associations with clinicopathological characteristics. The functional effects of MT-CO1 were evaluated in OSCC cell lines using gain-of-function assays. To assess the feasibility of pharmacologically targeting MT-CO1, molecular docking and subsequent molecular dynamics simulations were performed to characterize the interaction between amorolfine and MT-CO1; mechanistic rescue experiments were then conducted to determine whether the drug's effects were MT-CO1-dependent. RESULTS: MT-CO1 was associated with hypoxia and lactylation and was downregulated in OSCC, with lower expression correlating with poorer survival. MT-CO1 overexpression reduced cell viability, proliferation, and invasion while enhancing apoptotic signaling in vitro. Computational analyses further predicted a stable, high-affinity interaction between amorolfine and MT-CO1. Importantly, MT-CO1 suppression attenuated the antineoplastic effects of amorolfine in OSCC cells, supporting an MT-CO1-dependent mechanism of action. CONCLUSIONS: MT-CO1 as an underappreciated tumor-suppressive factor in OSCC and support further evaluation of amorolfine for therapeutic repurposing. MT-CO1 may serve as a biomarker of treatment response and that the MT-CO1-amorolfine axis may represent an actionable therapeutic vulnerability in OSCC.

item.title: Oral and Fecal Microbial Dysbiosis as Non-Invasive Diagnostic Biomarkers for Gastrointestinal Cancers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Accuracy.

item.description:
Authors: Hu S, Chen Z, Li Y, Liao Q, Luo M, Song D, Yu H, Gao Y, Yang S, Wan S, et al.
Journal: International journal of cancer | DOI: 10.1002/ijc.70779
Published: 2026-Oct-13

Abstract:
Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, including esophageal (EC), gastric (GC), and colorectal cancer (CRC), impose a substantial global burden, with early detection remaining crucial for improving patient outcomes. The oral and gut microbiota are increasingly implicated in cancer development and hold promise as sources of non-invasive biomarkers. However, current evidence on microbiome-based diagnostics remains fragmented, and a systematic comparison of the diagnostic accuracy between oral and fecal sampling across multiple GI cancer types is lacking. To address this gap, a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus up to December 31, 2025, identified 43 case-control studies (59 cohorts) comprising 4452 cancer patients and 5809 controls. The pooled area under the curve (AUC) was 0.846 (95% CI: 0.824-0.867), though with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 86.5%). By cancer type, pooled AUCs were 0.746 for EC (5 cohorts), 0.886 for GC (8 cohorts), and 0.850 for CRC (46 cohorts). A bivariate analysis of 20 cohorts comparing sample types found no statistically significant difference in diagnostic performance between oral (sAUC = 0.863) and fecal sampling (sAUC = 0.820; p = 0.369). While these exploratory findings suggest that oral and fecal microbial biomarkers may offer comparable diagnostic accuracy for GI cancers, with oral sampling presenting a more practical option for screening, the results are preliminary. Significant heterogeneity, a limited number of oral cohorts, and the absence of clinical control groups highlight the need for large-scale prospective studies with direct comparisons and real-world validation to validate these biomarkers for clinical translation.

Abstract:
Available epidemiological evidence shows that many cancers share familial risks, and this is increasingly confirmed by data on shared pathogenic germline gene variants between cancers. We decided to harness the world's largest resource on familial cancer to assess discordant familial risks for female breast (BC), prostate (PC), colorectal (CRC), and lung (LC) cancers with any of 22 different cancers in first-degree relatives (proband cancers). Familial relative risk was calculated as standardized incidence ratio (SIR) when either one proband or 2 or more (2+) probands were found in a family to distinguish low- and high-risk associations. Discordant familial associations of BC were significant for 12 1-proband and 5 2+ proband cancers. For PC, the numbers were 11 and 4; for CRC, they were 8 and 4; and for LC, they were 15 and 5. The results with large case numbers showed that BC, CRC, and LC associated with each other, but the familial association between PC and LC was negative. Many known or novel associations with possible genetic causes were found, including lobular BC with stomach cancer, PC with kidney cancer, CRC with squamous cell skin and thyroid cancers, and LC with gallbladder and endocrine tumors, the most common of which were parathyroid adenomas. Also, LC associations with esophageal and cervical cancers were unlikely to be due to smoking alone and require additional explanations. In conclusion, 2/3 of discordant associations could suggest low-risk genetic and environmental causation and 1/3 high-risk genetic causation, both waiting for experimental proof.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Odontogenic infections may progress to life-threatening complications if not managed promptly, and socioeconomic circumstances have been linked to their presentation, particularly where access to dental care is limited. Because every patient studied was already hospitalised, this analysis addresses the clinical type of infection at presentation, not the risk of developing one. Of 811 consecutive admissions, 525 were excluded: 509 for non-odontogenic conditions and 16 for records missing more than 30% of required clinical fields, leaving 286 complete records. Chi-square tests were reported with Cramer's V and Monte Carlo exact p-values where cells were sparse. Because the unpenalised model showed quasi-complete separation, the primary analysis was a Firth-penalised multinomial logistic regression, with abscess as the reference outcome. RESULTS: Adjusting for age, sex, employment, residence, recorded oral hygiene, systemic comorbidity and alcohol use, unemployment was associated with higher adjusted odds of Ludwig's angina (LA) and not abscess (AOR = 2.78, 95% CI 1.27-6.09), and rural residence with necrotizing fasciitis (NF; AOR = 3.62, 95% CI 1.33-9.80). Systemic comorbidity was associated with LA (AOR = 4.14, 95% CI 1.83-9.36), NF (AOR = 8.72, 95% CI 2.95-25.75) and cellulitis (AOR = 2.07, 95% CI 1.03-4.18). Sex and alcohol use showed no association. Number of children, the sole source of separation, was not retained; its penalised intervals included 1. CONCLUSION: Unemployment and systemic comorbidity were associated with more severe presentations, and rural residence with NF specifically. Findings are associational and describe variation in infection type among admitted patients rather than infection risk, within a retrospective single-centre design.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: This prospective study evaluated the impact of isthmus management (isthmus-sparing vs. isthmus-removing lobectomy) on postoperative hypothyroidism risk. METHODS: Between January 2022 and March 2023, 326 euthyroid patients with benign or low-risk papillary thyroid cancer were randomized into the isthmus-sparing (IS, n = 164) or isthmus-removing (IR, n = 162) group. Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Although antimicrobial mouthwashes vary in efficacy and safety for managing biofilm-induced gingivitis, concerns remain regarding their potential to reduce nitric oxide bioavailability and increase hypertension risk. METHODS: In this parallel randomized controlled trial, 90 participants were randomly allocated (1:1:1) to rinse with 10 mL of 2% saline (Group I), 0.2% chlorhexidine (Group II), or 0.1% octenidine (Group III) for 21 days. RESULTS: At day 22, antimicrobial mouthwashes significantly reduced clinical (29%-52%) and microbial (> 92%) measures (p < 0.001), whereas saline produced minimal changes (p > 0.05). Although systolic blood pressure increased slightly in all groups, the changes were clinically insignificant. Elevated pulse pressure in antimicrobial groups returned to baseline by Day 42. Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) or hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) and inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO) have more voice, cough, swallowing, GI issues, and MC activation than patients without ILO. METHODS: This retrospective study of 2162 patients meeting 2017 diagnostic criteria for hEDS (n = 507) or HSD (n = 1655) who were seen at the EDS Clinic in Mayo Clinic Florida from November 2019 to June 2025 compared patients who screened positive for ILO to those who screened negative. Patients were examined for self-reported symptoms of voice, cough, swallow, and GI issues as well as MC activation. RESULTS: Among patients with hEDS or HSD, 23.1% and 17.1% respectively screened positive for ILO. Patients with ILO had significantly more voice, cough, and swallow issues than patients without ILO (all p ≤ 0.007). Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Reliable biomarkers for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (R/M NPC) treated with immunotherapy remain limited. This study evaluated the association between longitudinal EBV DNA trajectories and clinical outcomes in patients with R/M NPC receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. METHODS: This post hoc analysis used data from a multicenter, single-arm, Phase II trial evaluating the programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor KL-A167 in patients with previously treated R/M NPC. Plasma EBV DNA was measured at baseline and at each scheduled efficacy assessment, which was conducted every six weeks until disease progression. EBV DNA trajectories were distinguished through a logistic trajectory model. Multivariable Cox models were used to calculate adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for survival outcomes. Compared with the persistently undetectable group, HRs of death were 4.96 (95% CI, 1.60-15.40) and 12.59 (95% CI, 4.01-39.51) for the fluctuating and persistently detectable groups, respectively. CONCLUSION: This study suggests that plasma EBV DNA trajectories could be a promising biomarker for monitoring treatment response and longitudinal risk stratification.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is used for reirradiation in recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (RM-HNSCC), but prognostic factors remain unclear. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 36 RM-HNSCC patients treated with CyberKnife-SBRT (2009-2022). ENDPOINTS: local control (LC) and overall survival (OS), estimated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 8.5 months, median OS was 9.6 months, with 1- and 2-year OS rates of 43.5% and 34.2%. One- and 2-year LC rates were 55.1% and 34.5%, with median time-to-recurrence of 14.1 months. CONCLUSIONS: Smoking history independently predicted LC and OS; larger tumor volume was associated with worse outcomes and may inform patient selection for SBRT reirradiation.

Abstract:

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The prognosis of patients with advanced biliary tract cancer progressing after gemcitabine-based first-line therapy remains poor. Effective second-line treatment options are limited, and outcomes with currently available regimens are modest. Trifluridine/tipiracil (FTD/TPI) and nanoliposomal irinotecan (nal-IRI) have demonstrated clinical activity in gastrointestinal malignancies and may provide synergistic antitumor effects. METHODS: TRITICC-2 is an investigator-initiated, prospective, open-label, multicenter, single-arm phase II trial conducted at academic centers in Germany. The study evaluates the efficacy and safety of FTD/TPI in combination with nal-IRI in patients with histologically confirmed, unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer who have progressed on gemcitabine-based first-line therapy. A total of 38 patients are planned for enrollment. Treatment consists of oral FTD/TPI administered on days 1-5 combined with intravenous nal-IRI on day 1 of a 14-day cycle, continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. item.title: Intratumoral Immunotherapy-The Future of Treating Merkel Cell Carcinoma?
item.dc:creator: Pande N, Moser JC, Chandrasekaran S, Brohl AS, Kulkarni RP, Ma VT
item.description:
Authors: Pande N, Moser JC, Chandrasekaran S, Brohl AS, Kulkarni RP, Ma VT
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193226
Published: 2026-Oct-07
PMID: 42882919



Abstract:
Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) represents a rare but highly aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer with limited systemic therapy options for patients who fail or are ineligible for immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Intratumoral (IT) immunotherapy has emerged as a promising strategy, leveraging the accessibility of tumor lesions and their inherent capacity to trigger immune responses, known as abscopal effects. This review synthesizes the current evidence on IT approaches in MCC, including Toll-like receptor agonists, cytokines, and oncolytic viruses, and highlights their distinct mechanisms of action, while emphasizing the critical need for standardized radiographic response assessment of injected and non-injected lesions. Inconsistent documentation of abscopal responses has hindered quantification of IT therapy's systemic potential, particularly in a disease where one-third of patients present with metastases and distant relapse is common. We outline MCC-specific rationale for routine lesion-level tracking, and recommendations for IT trial designs and objectives. Rigorous assessments of abscopal data will clarify IT's role as both rescue therapy and an ICI partner, potentially transforming outcomes in this refractory MCC.

item.title: From Molecular Alterations to Risk Prediction: Biomarkers of Actinic Keratosis Progression to Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Meyer T, Stockfleth L, Lang K, Käfferlein HU, Brüning T, Stockfleth E
item.description:
Authors: Meyer T, Stockfleth L, Lang K, Käfferlein HU, Brüning T, Stockfleth E
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193221
Published: 2026-Oct-06
PMID: 42882915



Abstract:
The high-and in most countries steadily increasing-incidence of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) represents a growing public health challenge. As the majority of cSCCs arise from pre-existing actinic keratosis (AKs), these lesions are recognized as the principal precursors of invasive disease. A comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms driving the progression from AK to cSCC is essential for advancing prevention, facilitating early diagnosis, and enabling targeted therapies. Moreover, this knowledge provides a basis for identifying biomarkers that can predict the risk of malignant transformation. The progression from AK to cSCC is a complex, multistep process driven by the gradual accumulation of genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental alterations. Over the past decades, numerous molecular changes associated with this transition have been identified. However, no single biomarker has demonstrated sufficient predictive accuracy for clinical use. This reflects the pronounced molecular heterogeneity of AKs as no individual alteration is uniformly present in all lesions that undergo malignant progression. In addition, numerous proposed biomarkers are also detected in non-progressive AKs and even in non-neoplastic skin, which compromises their sensitivity and specificity for predicting progression to cSCC. Current evidence, therefore, suggests that the most promising strategy for identifying AKs at greatest risk of malignant transformation is the development of a multi-marker panel. This panel, ideally, should integrate molecular signatures encompassing genetic, epigenetic, proliferative, inflammatory, and microenvironmental markers. This review summarizes the molecular factors that currently represent the most promising candidates for inclusion in such a multi-marker panel and discusses their potential clinical utility, while emphasizing the need for validation in well-designed prospective longitudinal studies.

item.title: Endoscopic Endonasal Approaches to Anterior Cranial Base Meningiomas: Indications, Limitations, and Surgical Decision-Making.
item.dc:creator: Chopra M, John D, Cote DJ, Zada G
item.description:
Authors: Chopra M, John D, Cote DJ, Zada G
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193217
Published: 2026-Oct-06
PMID: 42882911



Abstract:
Endoscopic endonasal surgery (EES) has fundamentally changed the management of anterior skull base meningiomas by enabling access to many lesions through a direct minimally invasive corridor that avoids traditional transcranial exposure. Improvements in endoscopic optical technology, surgical instrumentation, and skull base reconstruction have steadily expanded the range of tumors that can be treated through an endonasal approach. Even so, EES is not appropriate for every lesion, making thoughtful patient selection and surgical team experience the most important determinants of surgical success. This review explores where EES fits in the contemporary management of anterior skull base meningiomas, including olfactory groove, tuberculum sellae, and planum sphenoidale meningiomas, with particular attention to its indications, limitations, and situations in which EES may not be appropriate. Evidence comparing endoscopic endonasal and transcranial approaches for anterior skull base meningiomas is reviewed, with attention to how tumor anatomy, oncologic objectives, and individual patient characteristics influence the choice of approach. A major consideration is how surgical morbidity can be minimized without compromising oncologic and safety outcomes. Current strategies to protect critical neurovascular structures, reduce the risk of cerebrospinal fluid leakage, and improve skull base durability, including advances in vascularized reconstruction techniques, are discussed. Emerging outcome data and the evolving learning curve associated with EES are also reviewed. Rather than presenting EES as a universal solution, the evidence points toward a patient-centered approach in which operative strategy and clinical decision making is guided by tumor characteristics, anatomy, and surgical goals.

item.title: PET Tumour Segmentation in Head and Neck Cancer: Reproducibility, Reader Dependence and Concordance with CT-Defined Tumour Volume in a 154-Patient Cohort.
item.dc:creator: Pirson AS, Delahaut G, Georis R, Deheneffe S, Van der Vorst S, Kudura K
item.description:
Authors: Pirson AS, Delahaut G, Georis R, Deheneffe S, Van der Vorst S, Kudura K
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193214
Published: 2026-Oct-05
PMID: 42882908



Abstract:
Purpose: Volumetric PET biomarkers carry substantial prognostic value in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet their clinical implementation is hampered by segmentation heterogeneity. A fundamental and unresolved question is which segmentation method is most suitable for routine clinical use, both for a reader experienced in PET segmentation and for a reader without PET segmentation experience, such as an ENT surgeon or a radiation oncologist. This study addressed this question by assessing the intra- and interobserver reproducibility of four PET segmentation methods in MIM Maestro Software Version 7.4.2, identifying tumour-related determinants of variability, and examining concordance between PET-derived metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and CT-based gross tumour volume (GTV). Methods: Two readers with contrasting PET segmentation experience, a nuclear medicine physician experienced in PET segmentation (R1) and an ENT surgeon without prior PET segmentation training (R2), applied four methods to the primary tumours of 154 patients with HNSCC (oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx or larynx) treated with definitive (chemo)radiotherapy between 2010 and 2021: fixed absolute thresholds at SUV 3.0 and 4.0, a relative threshold at 41% of the maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax), and a gradient edge-detection algorithm (PET Edge+). R1 segmented twice with a washout of at least 4 weeks; R2 performed one session and delineated CT-GTV in the 85 patients whose PET/CT-derived CT served directly as the radiotherapy planning scan. The second session of R1 served as the reference for all interobserver and MTV-GTV analyses. Agreement was assessed by ICC (two-way mixed model), coefficient of variation, repeatability coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis; determinants of variability by a multivariable linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per patient. Results: All four methods demonstrated excellent intraobserver (ICC 0.993 to >0.999) and interobserver (ICC 0.989-0.996) reproducibility. SUV3.0 generated significantly more relative error than SUV41% (β = +3.1%; 95% CI 0.89, 5.3). PET Edge+ was the only method for which a significant method × reader interaction was observed in this reader pair: the reader without PET segmentation experience generated more error than the reader experienced in PET segmentation (β = +7.1%; 95% CI 3.9, 10), an effect concentrated in smaller tumours (below approximately 15 mL); in the 85-patient GTV subset, where tumours were larger on average, the interobserver ICC for PET Edge+ was 0.997. GTV concordance was good for three of four methods (ICC 0.808-0.895); SUV41% showed only moderate concordance (ICC 0.572). Conclusions: All four methods provided excellent volumetric reproducibility within a single clinical software platform, but they differed in reader dependence and in agreement with CT-defined GTV. Rather than supporting a universal segmentation standard, these findings suggest that the method should be selected according to its intended application, pending multicentre confirmation.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate (a) changes in caries experience, (b) changes in periodontal status, and (c) the need for dental extractions in a cohort of patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) and chemoradiotherapy (RTCT) for head and neck cancer (HNC). The sample mainly included oral, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers (89/113, 78.8%). Salivary glands, hypopharynx and other sites accounted for a minority of the cases (24/113, 21.2%). Seventeen patients (34.7%) experienced worsening of oral health status over time, which was associated with smoking (OR = 4.7, 95% CI: 1.27-17.37; p = 0.02). item.title: Cutaneous Neoplasms with Sebaceous Differentiation: A Comprehensive Update on Clinical, Histopathological and Molecular Classification.

Authors: Wiedemeyer K, Ferreira I, Adams DJ, Brenn T
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193209
Published: 2026-Oct-04

Abstract:
Cutaneous sebaceous neoplasms are rare adnexal tumours differentiated towards sebaceous glands, spanning a biological spectrum from benign (sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma, nevus sebaceus) to outright malignant (sebaceous carcinoma). Most tumours are sporadic and solitary, with a predilection for the head and neck of elderly adults, but a clinically important subset is observed in the setting of Lynch syndrome/Muir-Torre syndrome. Recent large-scale genomic and transcriptomic studies have provided insights into the pathogenesis of these unique neoplasms, revealing a genetically heterogeneous landscape shaped by mismatch repair deficiency, UV damage, and abnormalities in several other key signalling pathways. The inclusion of nevus sebaceus within the sebaceous tumour family in the WHO 5th Edition of Skin Tumours reflects a conceptual shift, recognising nevus sebaceus as a clonal, mutation-driven neoplasm and a precursor lesion for secondary tumour development.
